The **Fubini--Tonelli theorem** states conditions under which the order
of integration in a double integral can be exchanged.
We state two versions:
the Riemann version (@thm-fubini) is what applied courses usually use
for double integrals of continuous functions on simple regions;
the [$\sigma$-finite](measures.qmd#def-sigma-finite) measure-theoretic version (@thm-fubini-tonelli) is
included to make the
[joint-distribution form](https://morrison-lab.github.io/pds/expectation.html#cor-fubini-joint)
corollary in *Probability for Data Science*
follow from a stated theorem rather than from an aside.

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-double-integral}
#### Double integral

Let $f$ be a bounded function on a closed, bounded plane region $R \subseteq \reals^2$.
Cover $R$ with a grid of rectangles,
keep the $n$ rectangles that lie entirely inside $R$,
with areas $\change A_1, \ldots, \change A_n$,
and choose a point $(x_i, y_i)$ in the $i$-th rectangle.
The **double integral** of $f$ over $R$ is

$$\iint_R f(x, y)\,dA \eqdef \lim_{\norm{\change} \to 0} \sumin f(x_i, y_i)\,\change A_i,$$

where $\norm{\subdiv}$ is the length of the longest diagonal among the $n$ rectangles,
when that limit exists and has the same value
for every choice of grids and of the points $(x_i, y_i)$.
The symbol $dA$ stands for an element of area.

[@larsonCalc11e, Section 14.2]

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-double-integral-area}
#### The double integral of $1$ is an area

Let $f(x, y) = 1$ on the rectangle $R = [0, 2] \times [0, 3]$.
Every sum in @def-double-integral
adds up the areas of rectangles inside $R$,
and those sums approach the area of $R$ as the grid gets finer,
so

$$
\begin{aligned}
\iint_R 1\,dA &= 2 \cd 3 \\
&= 6.
\end{aligned}
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#def-iterated-integral}
#### Iterated integral

An **iterated integral** is an integral of an integral:

$$
\int_a^b \int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x, y)\,dy\,dx
\eqdef \int_a^b \paren{\int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x, y)\,dy}\,dx
$$

That is, integrate over the inner variable ($y$) first,
holding the outer variable ($x$) fixed,
and then integrate the result over the outer variable.
The inner limits $g_1(x)$ and $g_2(x)$ may depend on the outer variable,
or be constants $c$ and $d$, as in $\int_a^b \int_c^d f(x, y)\,dy\,dx$.
Iterated integrals in the other order, $\int \int \cdots \,dx\,dy$,
are defined the same way with the roles of $x$ and $y$ swapped.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-iterated-integral}
#### An iterated integral

Integrating over $y$ first, then $x$:

$$
\ba
\int_0^1 \int_0^2 x y\,dy\,dx
&= \int_0^1 \paren{\int_0^2 x y\,dy}\,dx
&& \text{(definition of the iterated integral)}
\\
&= \int_0^1 x \paren{\int_0^2 y\,dy}\,dx
&& \text{(} x \text{ is constant in } y \text{)}
\\
&= \int_0^1 x \sb{\frac{y^2}{2}}_{y=0}^{y=2}\,dx
&& \text{(antiderivative of } y \text{)}
\\
&= \int_0^1 2x\,dx
&& \text{(evaluate at the limits)}
\\
&= \sb{x^2}_{x=0}^{x=1}
&& \text{(antiderivative of } 2x \text{)}
\\
&= 1
&& \text{(evaluate at the limits)}
\ea
$$

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#thm-fubini}

#### Fubini's theorem (Riemann version)

Let $f$ be **continuous** on a plane region $R \subseteq \reals^2$.

1. **Vertically simple region.**
   If $R$ is defined by $a \le x \le b$ and $g_1(x) \le y \le g_2(x)$,
   where $g_1$ and $g_2$ are continuous on $[a, b]$, then

   $$
   \ba
   \iint_R f(x, y)\,dA
   &= \int_a^b \int_{g_1(x)}^{g_2(x)} f(x, y)\,dy\,dx.
   \ea
   $$

2. **Horizontally simple region.**
   If $R$ is defined by $c \le y \le d$ and $h_1(y) \le x \le h_2(y)$,
   where $h_1$ and $h_2$ are continuous on $[c, d]$, then

   $$
   \ba
   \iint_R f(x, y)\,dA
   &= \int_c^d \int_{h_1(y)}^{h_2(y)} f(x, y)\,dx\,dy.
   \ea
   $$

When $R$ can be described both ways, the two iterated integrals are
equal --- so the order of integration can be exchanged.

[@larsonCalc11e, Theorem 14.2, p. 982]

:::
